payload.title: Korean Traditional Wedding Customs Explained
payload.excerpt: Korean traditional wedding customs in the order many families live them: the ham, yedan and yemul, the wedding hall, the jeontong honrye, the wooden wedding geese, hanbok and the pyebaek, with what Australian couples need to marry in Korea or at home.
key_takeaways: Many Korean couples today hold a Western-style ceremony in a wedding hall, then change into hanbok for a short pyebaek with the groom's family.
In the full traditional ceremony, the jeontong honrye, the groom presents wooden wedding geese, often called Korean wedding ducks, to the bride's family before the couple bow and share a cup.
The ham, yedan and yemul are gifts between the two families, so agree early which exchanges you will keep and how simply.
As at November 2026, Smartraveller advises Australians to "Exercise normal safety precautions in South Korea", and the Australian Embassy in Seoul issues certificates of no impediment to marriage.

faq.a: A short traditional ceremony after the main wedding, where the couple bow deeply to the groom's family, receive rice wine and advice, and try to catch jujubes and chestnuts in the bride's skirt.

faq.q: What do you wear to a Korean wedding as a guest?
faq.a: Neat, modest clothes, such as a smart dress or a suit. Avoid white, which belongs to the bride, and anything too casual. Parents of the couple often wear hanbok, but guests rarely do.
Chukuigeum is congratulatory money given to the couple in a white envelope, handed to a family member at the reception desk. The amount is a private matter between the guest and the family.

faq.q: Can we hold a traditional Korean wedding ceremony in Korea as Australians?
faq.a: Yes. The legal marriage is a separate step: the Australian Embassy in Seoul issues certificates of no impediment to marriage, and the local district office can tell you how registration works. Confirm the documents and any fees with the district office and the Embassy before you book.

faq.q: What do the wooden ducks at a Korean wedding mean?
faq.a: They are wooden geese, often called Korean wedding ducks, which the groom brings to the bride's family in the jeonallye. Geese are a symbol of loyalty and fidelity, and wooden geese were given as a sign of the groom's everlasting love for his bride.

faq.q: Can we hold a pyebaek in Australia?
faq.a: Yes. Many Korean-Australian couples hold one after a Western ceremony, at the venue or the family home.
